questions.q: What makes a VAR(p) model genuinely different from fitting k separate AR(p) models, one per series?
options: VAR requires non-stationary input data, while AR requires stationary data
In VAR, every series' equation includes lagged values of all k series, not just its own past
VAR can only be fit with one series at a time
There is no real difference; VAR is just a naming convention
questions.explain: The defining feature of VAR is that each equation in the system depends on lags of every series in the system, capturing cross-series dynamics that separate univariate AR models would miss entirely.

questions.q: What does it mean if series A 'Granger-causes' series B?
options: A physically or economically causes B in a verified causal sense
Past values of A improve the prediction of B beyond what B's own past already provides
A and B are perfectly correlated at all lags
B's values determine A's values exactly one period later
questions.explain: Granger causality is a statistical, predictive concept: it tests whether including A's lagged values improves forecasts of B beyond using B's own lags alone. It does not establish true causation.

questions.q: What does an impulse response function (IRF) from a fitted VAR model show?
options: The in-sample AIC of the fitted model
How a one-time shock to one variable propagates through the system over subsequent periods
Whether the series is stationary
The Ljung-Box p-value for each equation
questions.explain: An IRF traces the dynamic effect of a one-time shock to one variable on itself and every other variable in the system over a chosen number of future periods, holding other shocks fixed.

questions.q: Before fitting a VAR model on raw, trending price levels, what should typically be done first?
options: Nothing — VAR handles non-stationary data natively with no adjustment
The series should be made stationary, e.g. by differencing, or a cointegration-aware model like a VECM should be considered
Convert the data to a single univariate series
Remove all but one of the series from the system
questions.explain: Like ARIMA, VAR generally requires stationary inputs. Non-stationary, trending series should be differenced first, or, if they're cointegrated and share a long-run equilibrium, a vector error correction model (VECM) is the more appropriate tool.

questions.q: In statsmodels, which function call directly tests whether one series' lags help predict another series in a VAR context?
options: acorr_ljungbox(fit.resid, lags=[10])
grangercausalitytests(df[['bond_ret', 'stock_ret']], maxlag=5)
ARIMA(df, order=(1,0,1)).fit()
arch_model(df, vol='Garch').fit()
questions.explain: statsmodels.tsa.stattools.grangercausalitytests runs the Granger causality test between two series at a set of specified lags, directly testing whether one series' past values help predict the other.
